question: When and where is the census ordered, and what criterion defines who must be counted?
Why are the Levites left out of the count, and what does the text say about their role at the tabernacle?
The verb פָּקַד (paqad) appears here as “number,” but it can also mean “visit” or “appoint”: what does this range suggest about being counted before God?
Each man is counted “by name”: what changes in you when you think that you are not just a number in the crowd?
How are the tribes arranged around the tabernacle, and which group is on the east and marches in front?
What does it mean that the tabernacle and the camp of the Levites set out “in the middle of the camps”?
The word דֶּגֶל (degel, “standard, banner”) marks each group of tribes: what role do banners and emblems play in each tribe's identity within the whole people?
The tabernacle occupied the center of the camp: what occupies the center of your life today, and is it what you would like to be there?
Who are the sons of Aaron, and what does the text recall about Nadab and Abihu?
What link does the text make between the Levites, the firstborn of Israel and the night of the exodus from Egypt?
Why does every בְּכוֹר (bekhor, “firstborn”) belong to the LORD, and how is the case of the 273 firstborn who exceed the number of Levites resolved?
The Levites are charged with guarding the tabernacle and its furnishings: what precious things have been entrusted to your care?
What age range is counted for the service, and what are Kohath, Gershon and Merari to carry?
Why must the Kohathites not touch or see the holy things, and what care must Aaron and his sons take so that they do not die?
The word עֲבֹדָה (avodah, “service, work”) is used both for manual labor and for worship: what does this say about carrying the boards, ropes and tent pegs of the tabernacle?
Some carry the ark, others carry tent pegs and ropes: how do you approach the tasks that seem less important in a shared work?
Who must stay outside the camp, and what reason does the LORD give for this?
What does the law of restitution require besides confessing the sin, and where does the compensation go when there is no relative?
How does the text describe the “spirit of jealousy,” קִנְאָה (qin'ah), and how do you read today a rite in which only the woman is put to the test?
Confessing and making amends with a fifth added: is there an offense of yours that calls for more than an apology?
What things does the Nazirite abstain from throughout the time of his vow?
What happens to the vow when someone dies suddenly near the Nazirite, and why are the previous days cancelled?
The term נָזִיר (nazir, “Nazirite”) comes from the idea of separating: in what sense is this separation “to the LORD,” and not just a withdrawal from things?
Which of the phrases of Aaron's blessing would you most like to hear spoken over you today, and why?
What does it mean that the priests “will put My name on the Israelites”?
What do the leaders bring first, how is it distributed, and why do the sons of Kohath receive no carts?
Why does the text repeat, almost word for word, the offering of each of the twelve leaders instead of summing it up in one sentence?
What does the chapter show about the role of each tribal נָשִׂיא (nasi, “leader”) in the dedication of the altar?
Moses enters the tabernacle and hears “the voice speaking to him”: what room do you set aside for listening, and not only for offering?
How were the seven lamps to be lit, and of what material and shape was the lampstand made?
What is the meaning of the Israelites' gesture of laying their hands on the Levites?
Why are the Levites themselves presented as a תְּנוּפָה (tenufah, “wave offering”) before the LORD?
At fifty the Levites leave the heavy work but keep helping their brothers: what does this say to you about the stages of life and of service?
What problem do some men bring to Moses about the Passover, and how does he respond?
What do the “second Passover” and the rule about the foreigner reveal about who may take part in the feast?
How does the עָנָן (anan, “cloud”) govern the rhythm of setting out and stopping, and what link does the text make between it and “the LORD's command”?
Sometimes the cloud stayed one night, sometimes a year: how do you deal with waits whose length is not in your hands?
What are the two silver trumpets for, and how are the blasts different from one another?
Why does Moses insist that Hobab go with them, if the cloud and the ark already show the way?
The verb תָּקַע (taqa‘, “blow”) applies to war and to feasts: what does it mean to be remembered “before the LORD” at the sound of the trumpets?
Moses' words when the ark set out and came to rest can serve as a prayer: how do you begin and end your journeys?
What do the people miss, and how do they speak about the manna?
What does Moses' complaint reveal about the weight of leading, and how does God answer it?
The word רוּחַ (ruach) is the Spirit placed on the elders and the wind that brings the quail: what link does the chapter suggest between the two?
Moses says “I wish that all the LORD's people were prophets”: how do you react when God uses someone from outside your circle?
What do Miriam and Aaron complain about, and what question do they ask about the way the LORD speaks?
What difference does the LORD set between speaking to a prophet in visions and dreams and speaking with Moses?
“Face to face” translates, in Hebrew, the expression “mouth to mouth,” with פֶּה (peh, “mouth”): what does this image suggest about the relationship between God and Moses?
Moses, called “very humble,” cries out for the healing of the one who spoke against him: how do you usually respond to unfair criticism?
What questions does Moses tell the spies to investigate about the land and about the people who live in it?
How does the spies' report go from “flowing with milk and honey” to a land that devours its inhabitants, and what changes between one statement and the other?
The verb תּוּר (tur, “explore, scout”) defines the mission of the twelve: what difference does the chapter show between observing the land and judging it?
The spies say “we seemed like grasshoppers in our own sight”: in what situation has the way you see yourself weighed more than the facts?
How does the congregation react to the spies' report, and what plan does it even propose?
What arguments does Moses use when interceding for the people, and what words about the LORD's character does he take up in v. 18?
What does the text mean by saying that Caleb “has a different spirit”?
The verb לוּן (lun, “grumble, complain”) returns several times: what does the chapter show about the effect of grumbling on a whole community?
After the verdict, the people decide to go up on their own: when have you tried to fix a mistake by repeating the disobedience by another route?
What rule applies to the foreigner who lives with Israel and wants to present an offering?
What is the difference between sinning “unintentionally” and acting “defiantly,” and why are the two cases treated so differently?
How should we read today the case of the man gathering wood on the Sabbath, placed right after the law about sinning “defiantly”?
What kind of fault is the שְׁגָגָה (shegagah, “unintentional sin”), and what way does the law open for the congregation and for each person?
The tassels served “so that you will remember all the commandments”: what concrete signs help you remember what is important?
Who rises up against Moses and Aaron, and what is their accusation?
The phrase “the whole congregation is holy, every one of them” sounds true: why, in this context, does it become an argument for rebellion?
According to Moses, what had the Levites of Korah's group already received, and what were they seeking beyond that?
The מַחְתָּה (machtah, “censer”) appears at three moments in the chapter: how does it go from an instrument of dispute to a memorial and a means of atonement?
Aaron stands “between the living and the dead”: in what conflict could you stand in the middle so that the harm stops?
How is the test of the twelve staffs carried out, and what happens to Aaron's staff from one day to the next?
Why must Aaron's staff be kept before the Testimony “as a sign to the rebellious”?
Why is the chosen sign a dry staff that פָּרַח (parach, “sprouts, blossoms”), and not a new punishment?
The people go from revolt to terror: “Are we all going to perish?”: how do you react when you perceive God's holiness?
What parts of the offerings are for Aaron and his family, and who may eat them?
What does it mean for the LORD to say to Aaron “I am your portion and your inheritance”?
To whom is the מַעֲשֵׂר (ma‘aser, “tithe”) given, and why must the Levites themselves also set apart a portion of what they receive?
The Levites were to offer “the best” of what they received: what would it be to give the best, and not the leftovers, in your life?
What features must the heifer have, and what is thrown into the fire with it?
Why do those who prepare the water of purification themselves become unclean until evening?
What does the “water of purification,” with the word נִדָּה (niddah), resolve, and why does contact with death require this rite?
Contact with death left a person unclean for seven days: how do you deal with grief and with the marks that death leaves?
Who dies at the beginning and at the end of the chapter, and where does each death take place?
What was Moses to do before the rock and what did he actually do, and why does the LORD say that he and Aaron did not believe?
The command was to speak to the סֶלַע (sela‘, “rock”): how does the word addressed to the rock differ from the blow with the staff, and why does it matter in the account?
Edom refuses passage to its “brother” Israel: how do you react when someone close to you shuts a door on you?
Why do the people grow impatient on the way, and what do they complain about?
What does it mean that healing comes from looking at a bronze serpent lifted up, and how is this episode taken up later in the Bible (John 3:14)?
What does the song of the בְּאֵר (be'er, “well”) celebrate, and who is remembered for having dug it?
The people admit “we have sinned” and ask Moses to pray for them: whom would you ask today to pray for you?
What does Balak ask of Balaam, and why does he think it would work?
If God tells Balaam “go with them,” why does God's anger burn when he goes?
The word מַלְאָךְ (mal'akh) names Balak's messengers (v. 5) and the angel of the LORD: what contrast does the chapter create between these two kinds of envoys?
The donkey sees what the seer does not: who in your life has noticed a danger before you did?
What does Balaam have prepared before each oracle, and how many times is this repeated?
What does v. 19 affirm about God in contrast with human beings, and how does this answer Balak's attempts?
How does the chapter play on the contrast between the verb בָּרַךְ (barakh, “bless”) and the request to curse?
“How can I curse those whom God has not cursed?”: is there someone you have been condemning more than God condemns?
What changes in Balaam's attitude before the third oracle, and what comes upon him?
How have the “star out of Jacob” and the “scepter out of Israel” been read in Judaism and in Christianity, and what does the text itself say about when this would come?
Why does Balaam, a foreigner, speak of the vision of the שַׁדַּי (Shaddai, “the Almighty”), a name of God linked to the stories of the patriarchs?
Balaam looks at the camp and says “How lovely are your tents”: what changes when you look at God's people as God sees them?
Where is Israel camped, and what do the people do with the daughters of Moab and with their gods?
What link does the text make between the zeal of Phinehas, the end of the plague and the “covenant of peace,” and how should we read such a violent act today?
The people “joined themselves” to Baal of Peor, with the verb צָמַד (tsamad, “join, yoke oneself”): what kind of bond does this word suggest?
The fall begins with invitations to banquets and sacrifices: what seemingly harmless invitations could draw you away from what you believe?
Who coordinates the new census, where is it taken and what is the counting criterion?
What does the text highlight by saying that none of those counted in the Wilderness of Sinai was among these, except Caleb and Joshua?
In a census of men, the שֵׁם (shem, “name”) of Zelophehad's daughters and that of Asher's daughter appear: what does this mention prepare for the following chapters?
“The sons of Korah, however, did not die”: what does this note say to you about not being bound by the mistakes of the previous generation?
Who are the daughters of Zelophehad, before whom do they stand and what argument do they use?
What does it mean that Moses brings the case “before the LORD,” and what does the answer change in the law of inheritance?
The verb עָמַד (‘amad, “stand, present oneself”) appears with the daughters of Zelophehad and with Joshua before Eleazar: what link does it create between the two scenes?
Moses asks for a leader so that the people will not be “like sheep without a shepherd”: what traits of leadership does this prayer ask for, and which of them could you exercise?
What is offered every day, and at what times of day?
Why does God call the offerings “My food,” and what does this suggest about the meaning of worship?
The תָּמִיד (tamid, “regular”) burnt offering is the base of all the other offerings: what does this word communicate about the rhythm of life with God?
Sabbaths, new moons and feasts marked Israel's time: what rhythms help you remember God through the week and the year?
What three solemn occasions of the seventh month does the chapter present, and on what days do they fall?
The number of bulls decreases by one each day of the feast, from thirteen to seven: what might this count indicate?
Why is the requirement of animals תָּמִים (tamim, “without blemish”) repeated so often, and what does it say about what is offered to God?
On the tenth day of the seventh month the people were to “humble yourselves”: what place do repentance and humility have in your life today?
What does v. 2 require of those who make a vow or oath to the LORD?
Why could the vow of a daughter or a wife be annulled by the father or husband, and how do you read this rule today?
What difference does the chapter make between the vow, נֶדֶר (neder), and the “pledge” someone binds on himself?
The vow of a widow or divorced woman stands on its own: what promise of yours, made to God or to someone, needs to be remembered or kept?
Who goes to war against Midian, how many men from each tribe, and who goes with them?
How can we read honestly the command of vv. 17-18, and what reason does v. 16 give for it?
The verb הָרַג (harag, “kill”) appears in the battle and then in the rules of purification (v. 19): what does it mean that even those who killed in war needed to be purified?
The commanders note that “not one of us is missing” and bring gold as an offering: how do you express gratitude when you are spared a loss?
Why do the sons of Reuben and Gad ask to stay on the east side of the Jordan?
Why does Moses compare their request to what the spies did at Kadesh-barnea?
What commitment does the verb חָלַץ (chalats, “arm oneself, be equipped”) express in the agreement between the two tribes and Moses?
“Be sure your sin will find you out”: what commitment left half done may be waiting for you?
Who wrote down the record of the journeys, and at whose command?
What does the text highlight about the exodus from Egypt, made “boldly” and with “judgments on their gods”?
The list repeats “set out” and “camped”: what does the verb נָסַע (nasa‘, “set out, pull up stakes”) say about the life of those who walk through the wilderness?
The inhabitants not driven out would be “barbs in your eyes”: what have you been tolerating that could become a thorn later?
What are the four borders of the land described in the chapter?
Why is the land described divided among nine and a half tribes, and where is the inheritance of the other two and a half?
The land is received with the verb נָחַל (nachal, “inherit, give as inheritance”): what does this vocabulary suggest about Israel's relationship with it?
Each tribe has a leader in the division of the land: in what decisions of your community could you help so that everyone is heard?
How many cities do the Levites receive, and how many of them are cities of refuge?
What criteria does the text use to distinguish intentional killing from accidental death?
Why can the manslayer go home only after the death of the high priest?
The verb גָּאַל (ga'al), which in Ruth describes the kinsman-redeemer, here names the “avenger” of blood: what does this role have in common in both cases?
The land must not be defiled because God dwells “in its midst”: how does this change the way you think about violence and justice where you live?
What concern do the heads of the family of Gilead bring to Moses?
How does the decision of the chapter balance the right of Zelophehad's daughters and the preservation of each tribe's inheritance?
Why does the word נַחֲלָה (nachalah, “inheritance”) appear so often at the end of the book, and what does it represent for each family of Israel?
The daughters of Zelophehad accept the new condition: how do you react when something you won has to be adjusted for the good of others?
